techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

resources.title: Contrastive Explanations Method (CEM) applied to MNIST — Alibi Explain
Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

sample_claims.text: For the invoices the risk model rates high, compliance reviewers judge that the pertinent positives are sufficient grounds for the rating and the pertinent negatives are events that would lower it.
For each flagged patient record, the pertinent positives and negatives match the findings clinicians use to tell the model's diagnosis from the nearest alternative.
On the instances tested, keeping only the pertinent positive leaves the model's prediction unchanged, and adding the pertinent negative changes it to a different class.
Each applicant declined for credit is told which absent factors, if present, would have changed the model's decision, and a reviewer has confirmed that each is something the applicant could change.
Caseworkers can tell an applicant which missing information, if provided, would change the eligibility model's outcome for that application.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

sample_claims.text: For 500 sampled refused applications, no counterfactual reached approval by changing only the postcode or another field on the agreed list of proxies for protected characteristics.

Every refusal letter issued since the model release contains at least two counterfactuals that change only features on the agreed list of applicant-changeable features, each re-scored against the model version in use on the day the letter was sent and confirmed to reach approval.

For 100 sampled patients, clinicians found no case in which the cardiovascular-risk classifier's counterfactuals, restricted to modifiable risk factors, reached a lower risk category through a change contrary to clinical guidance.
Re-running counterfactual generation with the recorded settings and seed reproduces the counterfactual sets given to applicants for all audited cases.

In a comprehension test of the draft refusal letter with 50 recent applicants, at least 80% named a change that would have led to approval, and at least 80% correctly said that the options do not guarantee approval if they reapply.
